title: Sign in to a workstation's test account with Ctrl+Alt+Delete and its PIN
instruction: Sign in to your workstation's test account: press Ctrl+Alt+Delete, type the account's PIN, 2580, and press Enter.
context: Signing in to an office PC is a daily act for anyone who works at a desk: where the Windows policy "Interactive logon: Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL" is Disabled, the lock screen asks for Ctrl+Alt+Delete first, which Microsoft says ensures users are communicating by means of a trusted path when entering their passwords. Windows accepts it only if Delete goes down while Ctrl and Alt are already held and still held. On a full-size keyboard no two of the three keys are adjacent: Left Ctrl and Left Alt are split by the Windows key, and Delete sits 29 cm away in the navigation cluster. So one hand must hold the pair down while the other strikes Delete, and then the PIN is typed key by key on the number pad and Enter pressed, without brushing a neighbouring key.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the desk. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left, z up; arm bases at y +305 and -305 mm. (1) A Logitech K120 wired keyboard (maker: 450 x 155 x 23.5 mm, 550 g, full-size US layout), loose on its four rubber feet, centred at x 330, y 10 mm, front edge toward the robot, Left Ctrl at the robot's left. Keys on the 19.05 mm pitch, 18 mm black caps with tops 23 mm up; the keys in play carry white legends (Ctrl, Alt, the Windows logo, Del, End, the number-pad digits, Ent). Centres (x, y mm): Left Ctrl (274, 212), Windows (274, 189), Left Alt (274, 165): Ctrl to Alt 47.6 mm; Delete (331, -76); number pad 2 (293, -157), 5 (312, -157), 8 (331, -157), 0 (274, -147), Enter (284, -195, a tall key). Every key in the bottom row, the navigation cluster and the number pad is a separate sprung cap: 2.8 mm travel (distributor datasheet), it registers at 2.0 mm, about 0.70 N there; the rest of the keys are fixed. Num Lock is on. (2) Behind it a 24 in monitor (panel 530 x 310 mm, its face at x 520) shows the Windows 11 lock screen asking for Ctrl+Alt+Del; a yellow sticky note on its bezel gives the test account's PIN, 2580. The PC's policy requires Ctrl+Alt+Delete. The lock screen gives way to the PIN prompt only when Delete goes down while a Ctrl and an Alt (either side) were both already down and are still held; each number-pad digit then adds a dot to the PIN box; Enter with 2580 opens the desktop, Enter with anything else clears the box and shows a wrong-PIN message. Nothing else is on the desk.
scoring: Read every control step from each modelled key's travel, the keyboard's pose and both grippers. A key is down while it is 2.0 mm or more in. Score 0 for the rest of the trial if the keyboard is lifted more than 5 mm or tilted more than 5 degrees (pulled off the desk; sliding it is harmless). Otherwise: 0.25 if a Ctrl and an Alt were down together for 0.5 s; 0.5 if the PIN prompt appeared (Delete down while a Ctrl and an Alt were both already down and still held; Delete first, all three in the same instant, or either let go as Delete goes down, does not count); 0.75 if after it the PIN was typed as 2, 5, 8, 0 with no other digit; 1.0 if Enter after the right PIN opened the desktop and, over the last 1 s, every key is up, both grippers are 30 mm or more from the keyboard and it moves under 1 mm. Capped at 0.5 if any other modelled key, a Windows key included, went down outside the act (before the prompt any key but Ctrl, Alt and Delete; after it any key but digits and Enter, the held Ctrl and Alt excepted), or Enter was pressed with a wrong PIN. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Success: 1.0 held for 1 s. Real trial: a Windows 11 PC with that policy, a K120 and an inline USB keystroke logger (KeyGrabber USB) that timestamps every key-down and key-up, plus the monitor in the trial video (lock screen, prompt, dots, desktop); the keyboard's lift by a rule at its corners on the video, tilt by eye; the 30 mm clearance with a spacer block on the video.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. Each modelled key is a cap on a sprung slider pressed only by fingertip contact: 2.8 mm travel to a hard stop (distributor datasheet), 2.0 mm actuation and 0.70 N there (estimates; measured on the trial's K120 with a force gauge and calipers before use). Feet friction 0.8 (est). The PC's response is a rule shown by sliding plates on the monitor; the real trial reads the real PC and the keystroke log. Legends are drawn only on the keys in play.
reset_notes: Lift both hands clear, sign the test account out (Win+L) so the lock screen shows, put the K120 back on its four tape corner marks, Left Ctrl at the robot's left, and check the sticky note still reads 2580 and Num Lock is on. Nothing is consumed.
